◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real data rarely fits a model exactly, so Ax = b often has no exact solution. Least squares finds the next best thing — the x that comes closest — and it is the mathematical engine behind linear regression, curve fitting, and much of statistics and machine learning.

When a system Ax = b has no solution (too many equations, noisy data), we find the x that makes Ax as close as possible to b. The trick: project b onto the column space, which leads to the normal equations.

The Normal Equations

Least-squares solution
The best-fit x solves the normal equations: ATA x = ATb. This x minimizes the total squared error ||Ax − b||² — the closest Ax can get to b.
🧠 ANALOGY

You want to hit a target that is out of reach (b is not in the column space). Least squares aims for the closest reachable point — the projection of the target onto where you can go. The leftover miss is made as small as possible, in the squared-distance sense.

Figure 1. b lies off the column space (it is unreachable). The least-squares solution gives Ax̂ = the projection of b onto the column space — the closest reachable point.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — set up the normal equations
For A = 111213 and b = 122, set up ATA x = ATb.
1
ATA = 36614 (sums of products of the columns).
2
ATb = 511 (each column of A dotted with b).
3
So the normal equations are 36614 x = 511.
Solving gives the best-fit line through the data points (this is exactly linear regression).
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 1. What equation do you solve to find the least-squares solution of Ax = b? And what quantity does it minimize? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Solve the normal equations ATA x = ATb. The solution minimizes the squared error ||Ax − b||² — the squared distance between Ax and b.

Solve AᵀAx = Aᵀb; it minimizes ||Ax − b||²
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. For A = 111 (a single column of ones) and b = 246, solve AᵀA x = Aᵀb. (Here AᵀA = [3] and Aᵀb = [12].) Work below.
Show worked solution

AᵀA = 1+1+1 = 3; Aᵀb = 2+4+6 = 12. So 3x = 12 → x = 4. (This is just the average of the b-values — least squares through a constant gives the mean!)

x = 4 (the mean of the data)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Least squares does not make Ax = b true — it finds the closest possible Ax. There is usually still a nonzero error (the data does not lie exactly on the model). The goal is to minimize that error, not eliminate it.

Key Takeaways
  • When Ax = b has no exact solution, least squares finds the closest x.
  • Solve the normal equations ATA x = ATb.
  • The solution minimizes ||Ax − b||² and projects b onto the column space.
  • This is the foundation of linear regression and curve fitting.
📊 FIGURE — Least squares: the line that minimizes squared residuals
Each residual (red) is the vertical gap between a point and the line: observed − predicted. The regression line is THE line making the sum of squared residuals as small as possible. R² then reports what fraction of the y-variation the line explains.
📊 FIGURE — when there is no exact solution
🎯 EXAM TIP
Least squares finds the best fit when the system is overdetermined — more equations than unknowns, so usually no exact solution. It minimises the squared residual, and the geometry is a projection: the best x is the one making Ax the projection of b onto the column space of A.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Projection finds the closest point in a subspace to a given vector — the heart of approximation and least-squares fitting. Gram-Schmidt turns any basis into a clean perpendicular one, which makes computations dramatically simpler (and is the basis of the QR factorization).

To project a vector onto a direction is to find its "shadow" along that direction — the closest point on the line. Gram-Schmidt uses projections to convert a set of vectors into a mutually perpendicular (orthogonal) set.

Projection onto a Vector

Projection
The projection of v onto u is projuv = ((u · v)/(u · u)) u — a scalar multiple of u giving the component of v along u's direction.
🧠 ANALOGY

Shine a light straight down onto a line: a tilted vector casts a shadow on that line. The projection is that shadow — the part of the vector that points along the line, with the perpendicular part removed. It is the closest the line can get to the original vector.

Figure 1. The projection (green) is v's shadow on the line through u. The dashed perpendicular is the part of v removed — the closest point on the line to v.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — project one vector onto another
Project v = (4, 2) onto u = (1, 0).
1
Compute u · v = (1)(4) + (0)(2) = 4.
2
Compute u · u = 1² + 0² = 1.
3
proj = (4/1)·(1, 0) = (4, 0).
projuv = (4, 0) — the horizontal shadow of v, as expected since u points along the x-axis.

Gram-Schmidt (the Idea)

Gram-Schmidt builds an orthogonal set: keep the first vector, then from each later vector subtract its projections onto the ones already chosen, leaving only the perpendicular part. The result is a mutually orthogonal basis spanning the same space.

✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Project v = (3, 5) onto u = (1, 0). Show your work.
Show worked solution

u · v = 3; u · u = 1. proj = (3/1)(1,0) = (3, 0).

proj = (3, 0)
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. Project v = (2, 6) onto u = (1, 1). (Use proj = ((u·v)/(u·u))u.) Work below.
Show worked solution

u · v = (1)(2) + (1)(6) = 8. u · u = 1 + 1 = 2. proj = (8/2)(1,1) = 4·(1,1) = (4, 4).

proj = (4, 4)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The projection formula divides by u · u (the squared length of the direction vector), not by v · v. Mixing these up is a frequent error. The result is always a multiple of u — a vector pointing along u.

Key Takeaways
  • Projection: projuv = ((u·v)/(u·u))u — v's shadow along u.
  • The projection is the closest point on the line to v.
  • Gram-Schmidt subtracts projections to build an orthogonal basis.
  • Divide by u · u, and the result is a multiple of u.
📊 FIGURE — Gram–Schmidt: subtract the shadow
Keep v₁. To orthogonalize v₂, subtract its projection onto v₁ — what remains (green) is exactly the part of v₂ perpendicular to v₁. Repeat against all previous directions, normalize, and an orthonormal basis appears.
📊 FIGURE — projecting v onto u
🎯 EXAM TIP
The projection scales u by (u · v) over (u · u) — the vector you are projecting onto, dotted with itself, which equals |u|². Both the numerator and denominator involve u; putting v · v underneath is the standard error, and it is only invisible when u happens to be a unit vector.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The dot product injects geometry into linear algebra — it measures lengths, angles, and especially when two vectors are perpendicular (orthogonal). Orthogonality underlies projections, least-squares fitting, Fourier analysis, and the "independence" of directions in data.

The dot product takes two vectors and returns a single number that encodes how aligned they are. From it we get length, the angle between vectors, and a clean test for perpendicularity.

The Dot Product

Dot product
For u = (u₁, …, uₙ) and v = (v₁, …, vₙ), the dot product is u · v = u₁v₁ + u₂v₂ + … + uₙvₙ — multiply matching components and add. The result is a scalar.

Length and Angle

Length and angle
The length (norm) of v is ||v|| = √(v · v). The angle θ between u and v satisfies cos θ = (u · v)/(||u|| · ||v||).
🧠 ANALOGY

The dot product is an "alignment meter." Point two arrows the same way and it is large and positive; make them perpendicular and it reads exactly zero; point them oppositely and it goes negative. Zero alignment — orthogonality — is the special value that matters most.

Orthogonality

Orthogonal vectors
Two vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular) exactly when their dot product is zero: u · v = 0. This is the algebraic version of a 90° angle.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — dot product, length, orthogonality
For u = (3, 4) and v = (4, −3): find u · v, ||u||, and decide if they are orthogonal.
1
Dot product: u · v = (3)(4) + (4)(−3) = 12 − 12 = 0.
2
Length of u: ||u|| = √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.
3
Since u · v = 0, they are orthogonal.
u · v = 0, ||u|| = 5, and the vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular).
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Compute the dot product of u = (1, 2, 3) and v = (4, 0, −1). Are they orthogonal? Show your work.
Show worked solution

u · v = (1)(4) + (2)(0) + (3)(−1) = 4 + 0 − 3 = 1. Since 1 ≠ 0, they are not orthogonal.

u · v = 1; not orthogonal
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. Find the length of v = (6, 8), and check whether (1, 2) and (2, −1) are orthogonal. Work below.
Show worked solution

||v|| = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10. For (1,2)·(2,−1) = 2 − 2 = 0 → orthogonal.

||v|| = 10; (1,2) and (2,−1) are orthogonal
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The dot product yields a scalar, not a vector — do not confuse it with anything matrix-shaped. And orthogonality is precisely u · v = 0; a small nonzero dot product means the vectors are close to perpendicular but not exactly.

Key Takeaways
  • Dot product: u · v = Σ uᵢvᵢ — a single scalar measuring alignment.
  • Length: ||v|| = √(v · v); angle: cos θ = (u·v)/(||u||·||v||).
  • Orthogonal ⇔ u · v = 0 (perpendicular).
  • The dot product brings geometry — lengths and angles — into linear algebra.
📊 FIGURE — The dot product and the projection

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Eigenvalues are not just abstract — they predict the long-run behavior of systems that evolve step by step: populations, web-link rankings, Markov chains, and coupled oscillations. The dominant eigenvalue often tells you where a system is headed.

Eigen-analysis shines on dynamical systems — anything described by repeatedly applying a matrix. The eigenvalues govern growth, decay, and the eventual steady state.

Powers and Long-Run Behavior

Dynamical system
A state that updates by xₖ₊₁ = A·xₖ evolves as xₖ = Aᵏx₀. Diagonalization makes Aᵏ easy, and the largest-magnitude eigenvalue dominates the long-term behavior.
🧠 ANALOGY

Think of a population split into age groups updated each year by a matrix. Over many years, the mix settles into a fixed proportion — the dominant eigenvector — and grows at a rate set by the dominant eigenvalue. The other eigenvalues fade away.

Symmetric Matrices Are Special

Symmetric matrices
A symmetric matrix (A = AT) always has real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors, and is always diagonalizable. This is why symmetric matrices are so well-behaved (and central to PCA).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — interpret eigenvalues
A dynamical system xₖ₊₁ = Axₖ has eigenvalues 1 and 0.5. What happens over many steps?
1
The component along the eigenvalue-1 eigenvector stays constant (multiplied by 1 each step).
2
The component along the eigenvalue-0.5 eigenvector halves each step, shrinking toward 0.
Over time the system approaches a steady state along the eigenvalue-1 direction; the other part dies out. (An eigenvalue of 1 signals a stable equilibrium — exactly how Markov chains reach their stationary distribution.)
✐ PRACTICE — concept

Show worked solution

The largest-magnitude eigenvalue, 2, dominates. Since 2 > 1, the component along its eigenvector grows without bound — the system grows (the 0.3 component fades away).

λ = 2 dominates; the system grows

Show worked solution

A equals its transpose (the off-diagonal entries match), so it is symmetric. That guarantees real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors, and that A is diagonalizable.

Yes, symmetric → real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors

It is the eigenvalue's magnitude that controls growth vs decay: |λ| > 1 grows, |λ| < 1 decays, |λ| = 1 holds steady. A negative eigenvalue (like −2) still grows in size while flipping sign each step — do not be fooled by the sign alone.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Diagonalization rewrites a matrix in its simplest possible form using its eigenvectors as a new coordinate system. This makes otherwise-painful computations — like raising a matrix to a high power — almost trivial, and it underlies solving systems of differential equations and analyzing long-run behavior.

If a matrix has enough independent eigenvectors, you can diagonalize it: write A = PDP⁻¹, where D is a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues and P holds the eigenvectors. In this eigenvector coordinate system, the matrix is just scaling.

The Diagonalization Formula

Diagonalization
A = P D P⁻¹, where the columns of P are the eigenvectors and D is the diagonal matrix of the corresponding eigenvalues. A is diagonalizable when it has n linearly independent eigenvectors.
🧠 ANALOGY

Diagonalizing is like rotating your viewpoint so a tilted ellipse lines up with the axes. In the right coordinate frame (the eigenvectors), the complicated transformation becomes simple stretching along each axis — which is exactly what the diagonal matrix D describes.

Why It Is Powerful: Matrix Powers

Because the middle terms telescope, Aⁿ = P Dⁿ P⁻¹ — and Dⁿ is trivial, since you just raise each diagonal entry to the n-th power. This turns repeated matrix multiplication into simple exponentiation.

Eigenvalues and eigenvectors reveal a matrix's "natural axes" — the special directions it merely stretches without rotating. They power Google's PageRank, principal component analysis, vibration analysis, and quantum mechanics. This is among the most important ideas in all of applied mathematics.

Most vectors get knocked off their direction when a matrix acts on them. But a few special eigenvectors only get scaled — stretched or shrunk along the same line. The scaling factor is the eigenvalue.

The Defining Equation

Eigenvalue and eigenvector
A nonzero vector v is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue λ if Av = λv — applying A just scales v by λ, leaving its direction unchanged.
🧠 ANALOGY

Imagine stretching a rubber sheet. Most arrows drawn on it get bent to new directions — but along a few special axes, arrows only get longer or shorter, staying perfectly aligned. Those axes are the eigenvectors; how much they stretch is the eigenvalue.

Finding Them: the Characteristic Equation

Characteristic equation
Eigenvalues solve det(A − λI) = 0. For each eigenvalue λ, the eigenvectors are the nonzero solutions of (A − λI)v = 0.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The null space, column space, and rank are the key subspaces and numbers attached to a matrix. They tell you what Ax = b can produce, how many solutions exist, and how much "real information" a matrix carries — central to data science, where rank measures effective dimensionality.

Every matrix A has two fundamental subspaces and a defining number. The null space is what A sends to zero; the column space is what A can produce; the rank ties them together.

The Two Fundamental Subspaces

Null space
The null space of A is the set of all solutions x to Ax = 0. It is a subspace of the input space; its dimension is called the nullity.
Column space
The column space of A is the span of its columns — every vector Ax can equal. The system Ax = b is solvable exactly when b lies in the column space.

Rank

Rank
The rank of A is the number of pivots in its row echelon form — equivalently, the dimension of the column space. It counts the independent columns (the "real information").
🧠 ANALOGY

Rank is the number of genuinely independent "knobs" a matrix has. If two columns are copies, turning one knob duplicates another — fewer effective controls. The null space collects all the input adjustments that produce no output change (the "dead" directions).

Rank-Nullity Theorem
For an m×n matrix: rank + nullity = n (the number of columns). Independent directions plus collapsed directions account for every input dimension.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — find the rank
Find the rank of A = 121243.
1
Row reduce: Row2 − 2·Row1 = (0, 0, 1). The matrix becomes 121001.
2
Count pivots: a leading 1 in row 1 (column 1) and a leading 1 in row 2 (column 3) — two pivots.
rank = 2. With n = 3 columns, the rank-nullity theorem gives nullity = 3 − 2 = 1.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A 4-column matrix has rank 3. What is its nullity? (Use the rank-nullity theorem.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

rank + nullity = n. So 3 + nullity = 4 → nullity = 1.

nullity = 1
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. Find the rank of A = 1326 by row reducing. Then give the nullity (n = 2 columns). Work below.
Show worked solution

Row2 − 2·Row1 = (0, 0). Matrix becomes 1300 — one pivot. So rank = 1. Then nullity = 2 − 1 = 1.

Formulas & method

For a matrix product C = AB, entry c(i,j) is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B: c(i,j) = Σ a(i,k)·b(k,j). The product is defined only when A has as many columns as B has rows.

Determinants

For a 2×2 matrix abcd, det = ad − bc. For 3×3, use cofactor expansion along any row or column, choosing one with zeros to save work: det = Σ (−1)^(i+j) · a(i,j) · M(i,j), where M(i,j) is the minor.

Inverse of a 2×2

A⁻¹ = (1/det) · d−b−ca, valid when det ≠ 0. Swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant.

Systems, rank, trace

📋 Systems of Linear Equations

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Linear Systems & Solutions

▸ Linear equation An equation of the form a₁x₁ + a₂x₂ + … + aₙxₙ = b , where the variables appear only to the first power. A system is several such equations sharing the same variables.

Gaussian Elimination & RREF

▸ Reduced row echelon form (RREF) A matrix is in RREF when: each leading entry is a 1 (a "pivot"), each pivot is the only nonzero entry in its column, and pivots step down to the right. From RREF, the solution is immediate.

Vector & Matrix Form

▸ Ax = b form The coefficient matrix A contains the coefficients, the unknown vector x lists the variables, and the constant vector b holds the right-hand sides. Multiplying A by x reproduces the left sides of all the equations at once.

"},"LINALG/cheat/c2":{"body":"

📋 Matrices

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Matrix Operations

▸ Addition Add matrices entry by entry — but only if they have the same dimensions . Scalar multiplication multiplies every entry by the same number.

▸ Transpose The transpose A T swaps rows and columns : the entry in row i, column j moves to row j, column i. Rows become columns.

Matrix Multiplication

▸ Matrix product The entry in row i, column j of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B — multiply matching terms and add. This requires A's columns to match B's rows: (m×n)(n×p) = (m×p).

Matrix Inverses

▸ Inverse matrix A⁻¹ satisfies A·A⁻¹ = A⁻¹·A = I . A square matrix has an inverse exactly when its determinant is nonzero ; such a matrix is called invertible (or nonsingular).

▸ 2×2 inverse formula For A = a b c d , the inverse is A⁻¹ = (1/det)· d -b -c a , where det = ad − bc. Swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant.

Elementary Matrices & LU

▸ Elementary matrix The identity matrix with one row operation applied . Left-multiplying any matrix by an elementary matrix performs that same row operation on it.

▸ LU decomposition Many matrices factor as A = L·U , where L is lower triangular (1s on the diagonal, entries below) and U is upper triangular (the result of forward elimination). The L records the multipliers used in elimination.

"},"LINALG/cheat/c3":{"body":"

📋 Determinants

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Determinant & Cofactor Expansion

▸ 2×2 determinant For A = a b c d , the determinant is det(A) = ad − bc — the product of the main diagonal minus the product of the off-diagonal.

▸ Cofactor expansion Expand along a row (or column): for each entry, multiply it by the determinant of the smaller matrix left after deleting its row and column (the minor ), with a checkerboard of + and − signs: + - + - + - + - + .

Properties of Determinants

▸ Determinant and invertibility A square matrix is invertible if and only if det ≠ 0 . A zero determinant means the matrix collapses space (rows are dependent) and has no inverse.

Cramer's Rule & Applications

▸ Cramer's Rule For Ax = b with det(A) ≠ 0, the i-th unknown is xᵢ = det(Aᵢ) / det(A) , where Aᵢ is A with its i-th column replaced by b .

"},"LINALG/cheat/c4":{"body":"

📋 Vector Spaces

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Vectors in Rn & Subspaces

▸ Subspace A subset H of Rⁿ is a subspace if: (1) it contains the zero vector , (2) it is closed under addition (sum of two vectors in H stays in H), and (3) it is closed under scalar multiplication . All three are required.

Span & Linear Independence

▸ Span The span of vectors v₁, …, v_k is the set of all their linear combinations c₁v₁ + … + c_kv_k. It is always a subspace — the smallest one containing those vectors.

▸ Linear independence Vectors are linearly independent if the only way to combine them to get the zero vector is with all coefficients zero (c₁ = … = c_k = 0). If some nonzero combination gives 0, they are dependent (one is redundant).

Basis & Dimension

▸ Basis A basis for a subspace is a set of vectors that is (1) linearly independent and (2) spans the subspace. It is the smallest set that generates the whole space, and every vector has a unique representation in it.

▸ Dimension The dimension of a space is the number of vectors in any basis for it. R² has dimension 2, R³ has dimension 3, and Rⁿ has dimension n. Every basis of the same space has the same size.

Null Space, Column Space & Rank

▸ Null space The null space of A is the set of all solutions x to Ax = 0 . It is a subspace of the input space; its dimension is called the nullity .

▸ Column space The column space of A is the span of its columns — every vector Ax can equal. The system Ax = b is solvable exactly when b lies in the column space.

▸ Rank The rank of A is the number of pivots in its row echelon form — equivalently, the dimension of the column space. It counts the independent columns (the "real information").

▸ Rank-Nullity Theorem For an m×n matrix: rank + nullity = n (the number of columns). Independent directions plus collapsed directions account for every input dimension.

"},"LINALG/cheat/c5":{"body":"

📋 Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors

▸ Eigenvalue and eigenvector A nonzero vector v is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue λ if Av = λv — applying A just scales v by λ, leaving its direction unchanged.

▸ Characteristic equation Eigenvalues solve det(A − λI) = 0 . For each eigenvalue λ, the eigenvectors are the nonzero solutions of (A − λI)v = 0 .

Diagonalization

▸ Diagonalization A = P D P⁻¹ , where the columns of P are the eigenvectors and D is the diagonal matrix of the corresponding eigenvalues. A is diagonalizable when it has n linearly independent eigenvectors.

Applications

▸ Dynamical system A state that updates by xₖ₊₁ = A·xₖ evolves as xₖ = Aᵏx₀. Diagonalization makes Aᵏ easy, and the largest-magnitude eigenvalue dominates the long-term behavior.

▸ Symmetric matrices A symmetric matrix (A = A T ) always has real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors , and is always diagonalizable. This is why symmetric matrices are so well-behaved (and central to PCA).

"},"LINALG/cheat/c6":{"body":"

📋 Orthogonality

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Dot Product & Orthogonality

▸ Dot product For u = (u₁, …, uₙ) and v = (v₁, …, vₙ), the dot product is u · v = u₁v₁ + u₂v₂ + … + uₙvₙ — multiply matching components and add. The result is a scalar.

▸ Length and angle The length (norm) of v is ||v|| = √(v · v). The angle θ between u and v satisfies cos θ = (u · v)/(||u|| · ||v||).

▸ Orthogonal vectors Two vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular) exactly when their dot product is zero : u · v = 0. This is the algebraic version of a 90° angle.

Projections & Gram-Schmidt

▸ Projection The projection of v onto u is proj u v = ((u · v)/(u · u)) u — a scalar multiple of u giving the component of v along u's direction.

Least Squares

▸ Least-squares solution The best-fit x solves the normal equations : A T A x = A T b . This x minimizes the total squared error ||Ax − b||² — the closest Ax can get to b.
